item.title: Push Your Musical Gods Off Their Pedestals
item.description:
“At this school, your teacher is your God.”

I can remember hearing this more than once while a student at the Curtis Institute of Music, several decades ago, but friends and colleagues who attended other conservatories have confirmed my suspicion that the sentiment was not specific to Curtis. In the music world, gods were everywhere: I’d already heard story after story in which teachers, conductors and soloists were praised as all-knowing and treated as all-powerful. I didn’t give it a second thought, despite having learned in Sunday school that it is dangerous to believe in false idols.

Today, as a grown-up musician myself, I find it to be an astonishing statement. Every one of my musical experiences — whether as a performer, teacher or simply a person trying to come closer to the music I love — leaves me more convinced that deifying teachers is wrong. It encourages deference and passivity, instead of the exploration and commitment that a true musician must spend a lifetime practicing.

All fields have teachers with worshipful acolytes, but it seems to me that musicians have a particular penchant for turning their teachers into deities. Why do we do it? A good teacher can offer invaluable guidance, but not a direct path to excellence and enlightenment, a route some would hope for. That is a myth. Being perpetually curious is hard work. Grappling with an unruly instrument and the infinite subjectivity of music is extremely hard work. This makes students susceptible to would-be gurus who purport to have all the answers and opens them up to different forms of mistreatment.

I recently contacted colleagues at the top of the profession about their experiences with harsh teaching. Stories of (usually at public master classes) humiliation came in quickly: a world-renowned pianist screaming at a student to stop after three notes; a violin teacher calling a student a racial slur; a legendary violinist advising a student to quit music; a venerated teacher comparing a student performance to bird excrement.

I’ve heard multiple teachers say that it is acceptable — even necessary — to beat up (figuratively, I presume) on their students. A celebrated violin teacher once told me that she did not consider it to be a true lesson until the student cried.

This approach should appall us, but we should also take time to consider what it says about our attitudes toward music and learning. You can browbeat people into obedience; you cannot browbeat them into understanding.

If we want musicians who engage deeply with the music they play, who approach it with imagination and courage and marry instinct to insight, then we should elevate teachers who acknowledge their own fallibility and who help their students learn to think and listen critically. If we want musicians who reduce their work to a set of rules to be followed, we should elevate teachers who think they can do no wrong and demand that their students think the same.

Famous teachers have connections that can open — or close — professional doors for their students. But this cannot fully explain why students and institutions are so in their thrall. There are plenty of powerful people in the music world, and not all of them consider themselves superhuman or abuse their power. We would not be so quick to excuse imperiousness or cruelty if we didn’t believe, erroneously, that certain people held the keys to absolute truth. The problem is not that some people are vicious: The problem is a musical culture so addicted to veneration that they are able to operate with impunity.

And operate they do. Recently, I saw the remarkable documentary “Dear Lara,” which tells the stories of (mostly) women who said they were sexually abused at a conservatory. The film makes a convincing and distressing case that the problem is systemic. Apparently, turning (mostly) men into gods can turn them into monsters.

I was lucky: None of my teachers were abusive. In fact, they were inspiring. I doubt that any of them believed for a moment that they knew everything. But I had absorbed that message, endowing them with a mystique they may not have wanted. If you asked me, in my student days, how my week had been, I would have responded by telling you how my lesson had gone. It was only one hour, but it was the hour that mattered.

Even then, though, I had an inkling that there was another approach. I knew on some level that the lesson could do no more than suggest possibilities, and that it would be my job, in all those other student hours, and all the years that would follow, to explore and develop and usually reject them, in the search for something authentic both to me and to the music I was playing. I knew that simply trying to please a teacher was the easy road, which is rarely the right one.

Being a musician means embracing complexity and ambiguity. It means living with all of the many possibilities a great piece of music suggests. This is often uncomfortable. It is human to wish for the complex to be simple, for the subjective to be objective. This wish can be so intense that people sometimes not only overlook poor treatment, they even welcome it. Several students have told me, to my amazement, that they want their teacher to speak to them in a way I can only describe as abusive. This phenomenon may even offer a hint about the appeal of authoritarianism — the bogus simplicity of its message justifying, for some, its inherent cruelty and even the ultimate inability to solve the problems it misdiagnoses.

Music-making should be a spiritual undertaking that requires lifelong devotion. Displacing this devotion onto a human avatar is alluring and wrong. It may make students feel safe, but it leaves them ill-prepared for their life’s work and creates an environment that can expose them to danger. As both a moral and an artistic matter, we must reject this path.

Jonathan Biss is a concert pianist.

item.title: Go Ahead, Sean Duffy. Let Your Daughter Go to Harvard.
item.description:
Take it from me, Sean Duffy: You can let your children go to Harvard. It will be good for them, and it will be good for Harvard.

Ordinarily I’m not in the business of weighing in on individual college decisions, but Duffy, the secretary of transportation, has made his family’s internal discussions as public as he possibly can.

The secretary has a reality television show (yes, you read that correctly), and last week a clip circulated online in which Duffy and his wife, Rachel Campos-Duffy, co-host of “Fox and Friends Weekend” and (along with Duffy) a former reality television star on MTV, talk about prohibiting their daughter from going to Harvard as an undergraduate.

The clip begins with Campos-Duffy saying that she’s “nervous” about her daughter, Paloma, going to Harvard. “We spent a lot of time nurturing and providing formation for our kids,” she said, “giving them an environment where they are steeped in faith and values.” It worried her to even think about dropping them off at a school that would “undermine that or try to undo all those things.”

The scene switches to a conversation between Duffy and Paloma, in which Duffy tells his daughter, “If I send you there, I think what happens is they have professionalized figuring out how they can take good young girls like you and I think corrupt their minds.”

Duffy told Paloma she didn’t have to believe what he believes, but he did not think that Havard gives students a “well-rounded picture” of competing ideas.

Paloma’s response was remarkably mature. “But I went to an extremely conservative school in high school,” she said, “and I’m part of an extremely conservative family, and then if I go to a liberal setting, that’s a way more well-rounded education than if I go to a conservative high school and then go to a conservative college.”

“But they’re so good at it,” Duffy replied. “You’ll see young people go to a conservative school with a conservative family, and they get perverted and contorted.”

Lots of people mocked the clip, but I had a different response; it was … relatable.

I had a very similar conversation with my father 35 years ago. We weren’t at the kitchen table. We were shooting hoops in our backyard as we pondered whether I should go to Harvard Law School. Like Paloma, I had grown up in a religiously and politically conservative home, and I had gone on to a religiously and politically conservative college.

Harvard was neither religious nor conservative. It was also in the midst of intense ideological battles, in which conservative students were sometimes ruthlessly booed, hissed and heckled, merely for stating their views.

I’ve also had different versions of this same conversation with Christian and conservative parents for decades — they look at the news of campus censorship, they see the left-wing monoculture (especially at elite universities), and they wonder if they’re sending their kids into the lion’s den. The concern seems especially acute with young women — that they’ll leave home as Laura Ingalls and come back as Lady Gaga.

Before you laugh at that idea, please realize that this perception is almost entirely the fault of elite educational institutions. They’re the ones that have created a left-wing ideological bubble. They are often extraordinarily intolerant of dissenting views. Peers and professors do sometimes make life difficult for conservative students.

I’ve experienced this myself, both as a student and as a lawyer. In my legal career I represented student after student who were subjected to a sometimes-shocking level of censorship, stigma and isolation at the nation’s most exclusive universities. Harvard has been one of the chief offenders.

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (I’m a former president of FIRE) currently gives Harvard an F rating for free speech, ranking it 245 out of 257 colleges and universities it measures. Sadly, 47 percent of Harvard students report self-censoring at least once or twice a month; 79 percent of Harvard students say that shouting down a speaker can be acceptable, at least in rare cases; and 32 percent say that using violence to stop speakers is also acceptable, again in rare cases.

That’s a sign of a sick free speech culture. That’s Harvard’s fault, not Sean Duffy’s. And no one should think that the environment is all bad. Conservatives will make liberal friends, including some who last a lifetime. My three years at Harvard were also three of the best years of my life, in part because they were so challenging.

In reality, the ideological monoculture is more harmful to liberals than conservatives. Paloma is right; given her conservative upbringing, exposure to very liberal students at Harvard would have given her a well-rounded education.

Her liberal classmates? Not as much. When you are surrounded by like-minded people, your ideas are less likely to be tested, and — just as dangerous — it becomes easier to believe that disagreement with you is a sign of ignorance or malice.

But here’s the key distinction: Intolerance is different from indoctrination. Radical peers, professors and administrators are far better at stigma than persuasion, and mockery does very little to change a person’s mind.

In fact, for Christian parents who are worried about their children’s faith, there is robust data showing that Christians with a college degree are more likely to attend religious services weekly.

All this becomes obvious the moment you actually meet college students. I’ve taught (and teach) at both the college and law-school level, in both religious and elite secular universities, and not once did I perceive my students as little lumps of clay, ready to be molded however I pleased. Instead, my students are people of conviction. The best students are full of both conviction and curiosity. They’re eager to learn. The worst have conviction without curiosity. They’re eager to tell me exactly what they think I’m doing wrong.

I’m convinced that every person — especially those of us who live in the world of ideas — should spend time in a place where he or she is a distinct religious or ideological minority, even when it’s hard. It can be among the most clarifying and rewarding experiences in life.

In a conversation last week between MSNow’s Katy Tur, my friend Mona Charen and me, Mona, the policy editor at The Bulwark, reflected on her own experience as a conservative at Barnard College in the 1970s. She referred to a quote of John Stuart Mill’s: “He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.”

When I was in law school, I appreciated the fact that my ideas were being tested by the smartest people I’d ever met. There was no way for me to skate through a conversation — much less a class. That was worth the scorn, as annoying and painful as that scorn could sometimes be.

But few things taught me that I belonged there more than those moments when my classmates would say, “I’ve never heard that argument before” or “I’ve never even met anyone like you before.”

We learned from one another, and we still learn from one another. There are times when my friends and classmates can even hear the echoes of our longtime debates and disagreements in my columns. I was a conservative and a Christian when I met them. I’m a conservative and a Christian now, but I’m a better Christian and a better conservative because they tested me. In the absence of that testing, I shudder to think what I’d be like today.

To see what right-wing bubbles can do to the Christian mind, one need only look at the strident, conspiratorial — and often downright dumb — discourse in so many parts of the religious right today.

None of Harvard’s sins justify the Trump administration’s attacks on its academic freedom. And I absolutely wonder why a secretary of transportation has a reality television show, but no one should mock Duffy for his concern for his daughter’s spiritual welfare. Watching that moment (however scripted it was) did give you an insight into countless conversations in conservative homes across the country.

That conversation with my father many years ago was also hard. And it was more than a little sad. I wasn’t just leaving my home. In many ways, I was also separating from the denomination I grew up in. I was leaving my home and my spiritual family. There were precious few churches of Christ in greater Boston. I think any parent can understand this concern.

But we made the decision together. I was going to go. It was going to be hard (I didn’t know a single soul within roughly 700 miles of Cambridge, Mass.), but I went because of my faith, not in spite of it. My father and I quoted the words of the Apostle Paul to each other, which were written in an infinitely more perilous time for Christians. I told you I was from a conservative Christian family.

“God has not given us a spirit of fear,” Paul writes in Second Timothy, “but of power and of love and of a sound mind.”

item.title: It’s One of Our Greatest and Most Controversial Novels. How Should It Be Taught?
item.description:
A few years ago, I created a seminar for my students at Columbia University, where I teach writing, about the challenges of separating a novel’s literary value from its politics. There were 10 books on the syllabus, including “Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.”

Even though I hadn’t read the novel since I was a child, I knew it had to be part of this course. For more than a century, Mark Twain’s saga of a young white boy and an enslaved Black man traveling on a raft down the Mississippi River has been a fixture of the American canon. Narrated in Huck’s cheeky, irrepressible voice, it pioneered the writing of literary fiction in the vernacular while mercilessly skewering the racism and hypocrisy of white Southerners in the pre-Civil War era. Influential critics from T.S. Eliot to Ralph Ellison enshrined it as essential — not just a great book but, in the words of Lionel Trilling, “one of the central documents of American culture.” By the end of the 1940s, it had become a mainstay of anthologies and survey classes.

But over the past few decades, this once-standard text has come to occupy a slippery position in the classroom. Some perceive it as an essential commentary on slavery’s depredations, while others feel it endangers Black students — mainly because the racist slur known euphemistically as the N-word appears more than 200 times. A son of slave owners who married into a prominent abolitionist family, Twain almost certainly intended the novel as an indictment of racial prejudice and used the word to illustrate the racism of his characters, not to endorse it. Though Huck, indoctrinated in the conventional morality of his time, initially believes it’s wrong to help an enslaved person escape, he comes to feel loyalty and love for Jim, his companion. The tension animating the story is not just whether the two of them can outwit the villains who want to capture Jim, but also whether Huck will reject his prior conception of right and wrong.

Still, many readers understandably feel that the novel’s constant, even obsessive repetition of the slur reinforces the system of white supremacy that it purports to critique. In the classroom, where teachers often read aloud or call on their students to do so, the problem is obvious. Even when the word isn’t spoken, its silently menacing presence on the page is impossible to ignore.

I could see this as soon as I opened the book. I was reading a used copy whose previous owner must have been a student. This person started out diligently highlighting and taking notes. But they clearly found the slur upsetting. “OMG stop using it,” they wrote in the margin at one point. Eventually, the highlights and notes petered out.

I gulped down the novel in two sittings, disoriented and amazed. It felt genuinely shocking to be confronted by the slur so brazenly. But I was beguiled by Huck’s plain-spoken voice and by the way Twain uses it to point to the gap between the character’s limited understanding of the world and what is really taking place in the novel, which we must work out on our own. “It shows how a body can see and don’t see, at the same time,” Huck says at one point when he’s failed to notice something — a line that could be the novel’s motto. I was startled, too, to find that Twain relies on Jim as the novel’s moral fulcrum, often leaving space in the narrative for a richer and more multilayered reading of the character than is commonly thought. Despite all its problems, the book felt fresh and relevant. Reading it, I wished Twain were alive and writing today, if only to know what he would make of our current president.

Since 2000, “Huck Finn” has been challenged or banned by school districts in at least 12 states, usually because it is perceived as racist. At the Mark Twain House and Museum in Hartford, Conn., the book sits front and center on a shelf of banned books displayed in a literal cage. But educators tell me the book is less likely to be formally removed from curriculums than simply put aside by overworked teachers who have neither the classroom time nor the intellectual energy to handle a text widely seen as radioactive — and who fear that a misstep could cost them their jobs. “They haven’t banned it,” says John Conway, a retired public school teacher in Alabama. “They just don’t want to have the discussions about it.”

A majority of book challenges today come from right-wing activists, organizations and government officials who object to what they see as progressive political content, particularly regarding race and L.G.B.T.Q. issues. Precisely because it deals with the history of enslavement, “Huck Finn,” too, is now vulnerable to such challenges. Early in his second term, President Trump issued an executive order titled “Ending Radical Indoctrination in K-12 Schooling,” which directs schools to promote “patriotic education,” defined as “an accurate, honest, unifying, inspiring and ennobling characterization of America’s founding and foundational principles.” This executive order explicitly prohibits what it calls “discriminatory equity ideology,” a term that seems to cover just about any discussion of systemic racism — the novel’s central engine.

In this climate, it’s easy to see why “Huck Finn” is “dying a quiet death,” as one teacher tells me. Owing to a combination of factors — the early introduction of technology in the classroom, pandemic learning losses and now the growing use of A.I. — students are reading more reluctantly than ever before. Where teachers once assigned multiple novels per year, they are now likely to cover only one or two. At the same time, novels by Black writers that deal with racism, such as Zora Neale Hurston’s “Their Eyes Were Watching God,” have become staples of the curriculum.

The Twain scholar and Stanford professor Shelley Fisher Fishkin compares “Huck Finn” to fugu, a Japanese delicacy so poisonous that a chef must be specially licensed to serve it. “If it’s prepared right, it’s phenomenal,” she says. “If it’s taught wrong, it can be toxic.” What might it mean for the book to be “prepared right”?

Over the past few years, I’ve been speaking to teachers and students who believe that “Huck Finn” still has a necessary place in the classroom, because it is uniquely able both to convey the structures of racism embedded in American society and to model how prejudice can be overcome. The book provides its own master class in critical thinking; as Toni Morrison wrote in an admiring introduction to the 1996 Oxford edition, “The brilliance of ‘Huck Finn’ is that it is the argument it raises.” Watching teachers and their students grapple with it, and grappling with it myself, I came to feel that the book remains vital. Huck’s journey to political and ethical independence serves as a powerful testament to the importance of questioning authority and trusting oneself, a primary American principle that remains at least as urgent now as it was in Twain’s time. As one teacher told me, “It’s about the country’s search for a soul.”

Anyone who wants to teach “Huck Finn” must figure out how to handle the slur, which first appears in Chapter 1. Huck, whose father is the town drunk, has grown up enviably free from parental interference, sleeping outdoors and rarely going to school. When the story begins, he has been quasi-adopted by the Widow Douglas, who is trying to “sivilize” him (Huck’s term). After she delivers a lecture about how to get into heaven, Huck describes their nighttime routine: “By and by they fetched the niggers in and had prayers, and then everybody was off to bed.”

The word was still part of common colloquial language at the time of the story — the novel, published in 1884, is set “forty to fifty years ago” — but it was understood to be offensive. Twain grew up hearing it all around him but is said to have no longer used it when writing in his own voice by the time he was writing the novel. His use of it in characters’ speech is at once a realistic portrayal of how some Southerners would have talked and a literary device highlighting the degradation of a society that believed itself to be “sivilized” while persisting in stunningly barbaric behavior. It’s no accident that he often puts it in the mouth of a character espousing religion, one of the main targets of the book’s satire. “Twain did not set out in that book to write a story about an epithet,” says Joseph Csicsila, a white professor in Michigan. “The epithet figures in that book as a function of character revelation.”

This intellectual explanation doesn’t mitigate students’ distress when encountering the word. “Reading ‘Huckleberry Finn’ was like seeing a Confederate statue,” Randall Dottin, a documentary filmmaker who is Black, tells me of his experience with the book in high school several decades ago. “No student wants to hear it,” says Ryan Heryford, a college professor in California, who still remembers his own discomfort as a white student asked to read aloud from the book. “It’s a form of violence.” Rohan Pai, an Indian American student who read the book in high school, concurs: “It was obviously a little tense when someone would get to that word.”

In the early 2000s, Alan Gribben, a white professor of English who died in May, noticed that his Black students tended to be absent when he taught the novel. Hoping to “retain a great work and take some of the pain out of it,” he decided to create a new edition that replaced the slur with “slave.” He brought his manuscript to NewSouth Books, then an independent publisher in Montgomery, Ala. (It is now part of the University of Georgia Press.)

When the NewSouth edition of “Huck Finn” was first announced in 2011, it was pilloried. Twain scholars accused Gribben of censoring the work of an American icon, while editorialists attacked his work as political correctness gone wild. In an op-ed, the Twain biographer Ron Powers charged him with the “evisceration” of a classic. Fishkin, the Stanford scholar, was more measured but equally disapproving, arguing that Gribben’s edits neutered the book: “To expose a racist society for what it is, you have to show racists as they are, speaking as they would speak,” she wrote.

Fifteen years later, the tide has shifted. No teacher I’ve met speaks the slur aloud in the classroom or allows students to do so. Instead, they substitute “N-word” or a nonverbal sound like “mm.”

“Knowing that such a thing existed, it felt derelict to me to choose any other version” than the NewSouth edition, says Peter Mergenthaler, an English teacher in Washington, D.C., who is white. To have the word on the page “for kids to see, to read independently and either to misunderstand contextually or be grievously hurt by it — I don’t know that even with dozens of years of experience I would choose the uncensored version,” he adds. Maya Dunkley, one of his students, agrees with this approach. “You don’t have to read racism to learn about racism and learn that it’s wrong,” Maya, who identifies as biracial, tells me.

But most of the teachers I spoke to felt that Gribben’s effort, while well-intentioned, was misguided. The educator and scholar Jocelyn A. Chadwick, who is Black and has written extensively about pedagogy as well as about Twain and race, argues that it’s better for an inexperienced teacher not to teach the novel at all than to use the NewSouth edition. The slur, she says, is essential to the book. “It’s not a hip-hop word, it’s not a slang word, it’s a word that’s so filled with blood and agony and hatred,” she says, adding: “It’s supposed to hurt.” Eyob Sisay, a Black student from Washington, D.C., agrees. “Just knowing how jarring it is, and how casually and frequently it’s used in the story, I think it’s important for us to have that perspective,” he says.

Samantha Goodwin, who taught Eyob at Sidwell Friends School in Washington, spends several class periods contextualizing the slur, using the work of the linguist Geneva Smitherman and the historian Elizabeth Stordeur Pryor. I sat in on one of her classes as she walked her students through the difference between milder Horatian satire, which is meant to be funny, and Juvenalian satire, the harshest form of the device, which Twain uses for his sharpest critiques. “It’s not meant to make you feel good,” she told me. It’s meant to make the reader uncomfortable — and angry.

Twain’s use of the word is part of his assault on the hypocritical mores of supposedly genteel Southern society. People Huck and Jim encounter over the course of the novel — many of whom Huck believes he should respect as “quality” — participate in a blood feud that results in the deaths of multiple people, including children; try to swindle three grieving sisters out of their inheritance; and speak of Black people as less than human. “If you read it without understanding that it’s satire, your anger will be directed at the author,” Goodwin cautioned. This is exactly what often happens when students first encounter “Huck Finn.”

As the students debated where various scenes in the novel fall on the satirical spectrum, Goodwin, who is white, brought up Huck’s demeaning language about Black people. There was a pause in which I could see the discomfort on some students’ faces. Finally, a white student responded. “It’s supposed to anger you,” he said. “You feel like Huck has been taught that Black people aren’t human.”

“You’re speaking nicely to the power of Huck as narrator,” Goodwin responded. “He doesn’t have the ability to take the next step and say: ‘Wait a second. Why did I believe that?’ But we get angry.”

In a pedagogical culture that tends to shy away from unpleasantness, Goodwin’s approach felt like an honest — and valuable — way of dealing with one of the ugliest aspects of American literary history. Reading “Huck Finn” isn’t just an intellectual experience; it’s also an emotional journey. If the book produces strong feelings in its readers, it’s doing what it’s supposed to do.

Still, I left Goodwin’s classroom wondering whether her strategy was replicable on a larger scale. She teaches in an elite private school where around 40 percent of students are white, and she is able to design her own curriculum. It’s easy to see how the social dynamics could spin out of control in a classroom led by a teacher with less experience or skill or fewer resources. She thinks her own children, who are biracial, should wait until at least the age of 14 to read the novel.

And even Goodwin can’t persuade all her students of the book’s value. At the end of every school year, when she asks them — anonymously — whether it should still be taught, some say no: “It’s just racist.”

In addition to the slur, Twain’s characterization of Jim is another reason some readers perceive “Huck Finn” as racist. The character speaks in heavy dialect that sounds similar to portrayals of Black people in minstrel shows. Sometimes he seems to function as a foil to Huck, expressing confusion over simple facts or misunderstanding well-known stories, such as the parable of King Solomon and the baby. In one classroom I visited, students debated whether he was intended to serve as comic relief.

It sometimes seems that way. In Chapter 2, Huck and Tom Sawyer are trying to sneak out of the widow’s house. Huck stumbles and attracts the attention of Jim, who goes outside and stops just at the spot where the boys are hiding. “Dog my cats ef I didn’ hear sumf’n … I’s gwyne to set down here and listen tell I hears it agin,” he says, apparently to himself. Positioning himself nearly on top of the boys, he falls asleep, allowing them to escape.

Percival Everett’s 2024 novel “James,” which won both the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award, loosely retells the story of “Huck Finn” from Jim’s perspective. Everett’s version of the character sometimes seems tailor-made to compensate for the apparent flaws in Twain’s depiction. Not only has he secretly taught himself to read and write, but he holds erudite fantasy conversations with Enlightenment philosophers. When he uses dialect, it’s a canny survival strategy, giving white people a version of Black people they can feel superior to. “More than a correction, it’s a rescue mission,” Sam Sacks wrote in The Wall Street Journal.

But in the gap between Huck’s narration and what is actually going on, Twain allows the reader to enter into Jim’s perspective — and to notice how other characters do not. Robert Paul Lamb, author of the forthcoming “Huck and Jim’s America: Slavery, Race and Realism in Mark Twain’s World,” speculates that Jim’s performative language in the first scene suggests he’s only pretending to be asleep in order to amuse the boys — which is also the way Everett rewrites the episode. In “Jim: The Life and Afterlives of Huckleberry Finn’s Comrade,” published last year, Fishkin argues that Jim’s actions demonstrate he is more intelligent and resourceful than Huck appreciates. “Start with the assumption that Jim is smart,” she tells her students. “Once that seed is planted, they begin to recognize Huck’s blind spots.” A body can see and don’t see, at the same time.

A first-person narrative, by definition, is limited to the point of view of the person who is telling the story. The fact that the novel is narrated in Huck’s exceedingly unreliable voice means Twain can’t give us Jim’s point of view on anything. But when things happen that Huck has no words to express — because they are beyond his comprehension or involve a leap of empathy that he can’t yet make — Twain indicates that by leaving him silent. Toni Morrison described these moments as “when scenes and incidents swell the heart unbearably precisely because unarticulated, and force an act of imagination almost against the will.”

Morrison may have been thinking of the end of Chapter 23, one of the book’s most poignant episodes. One morning Huck finds Jim weeping with longing for his wife and children. At the time, defenders of slavery often justified separating families by saying that Black people’s family ties were not as strong as white people’s. It suddenly strikes Huck that this is a lie. “I do believe he cared just as much for his people as white folks does for theirn,” he muses. It’s a shocking line — and a moment when we might need to remind ourselves that Twain is representing such ideas rather than endorsing them. Much of the novel’s extraordinary energy comes from the tension between Huck’s dawning sense of morality and the inadequacy of his language to convey it.

Then Jim tells a wrenching story. One day, shortly after his daughter recovered from scarlet fever, she ignored an order that he gave her, and he struck her hard across the face in rage. A few minutes later, when she failed to react to a loud noise, he realized the disease had left her deaf. He castigated himself for treating his child — a child he may never see again — so harshly and unfairly. “O de po’ little thing! de Lord God Amighty fogive po’ ole Jim, kaze he never gwyne to fogive hisself as long’s he live!” Jim recalls saying. “O, she was plumb deef en dumb, Huck, plumb deef en dumb — en I’d ben a treat’n her so!”

The chapter ends there, without comment from Huck. Just Jim’s words, with all their pain, for the reader to endure.

“If you were to say to Mark Twain today, ‘You were a racist,’ he probably would agree with you,” John Pascal told a class of 11th graders at Seton Hall Preparatory School, an all-boys Catholic high school in New Jersey. Before Pascal’s students even opened “Huck Finn,” he walked them through Twain’s life story, focusing on the writer’s about-face with regard to slavery and the close relations he had with Black people, including Frederick Douglass. Pascal, who is white, especially likes to tell the story of Warner T. McGuinn, a Black student at Yale Law School whose tuition Twain paid — a gesture many see as an attempt at reparations for slavery. “People who say ‘Huck Finn’ is racist, and Mark Twain is racist, don’t know this fact,” Pascal told his students.

On this spring morning, they were working through Chapter 15, one of the thorniest passages. Huck and Jim have been looking for the point where the Mississippi and Ohio Rivers converge. They plan to stop there and find a steamboat to take them up into the free states. The river is enveloped in fog and full of debris, and when Huck paddles ahead in a canoe to look for a place to anchor the raft, he can’t find his way back. When he finally returns the next morning, Jim is overjoyed to see him. But Huck, who can rarely resist playing a mean trick, tries to convince Jim that he dreamed the entire episode.

The students were at first too focused on decoding Jim’s speech to appreciate the emotional dynamics. “Goodness gracious, is dat you, Huck? En you ain’ dead — you ain’ drownded — you’s back agin?” one of the boys read haltingly as others snickered.

Jim finally concedes and even offers an interpretation of the supposed dream, but Huck can’t stop there. “What does these things stand for?” he asks, pointing to the leaves and branches that accumulated on the raft during the stormy night.

Now Jim understands that Huck was fooling him. “When I got all wore out, wid work, en wid de callin’ for you, en went to sleep, my heart wuz mos’ broke bekase you wuz los’,” he tells Huck. “En all you wuz thinkin’ ’bout, wuz how you could make a fool uv ole Jim wid a lie. Dat truck dah is trash; en trash is what people is dat puts dirt on de head er dey fren’s en makes ’em ashamed.”

This speech constitutes the most important education Huck receives from anyone in the entire novel. At a time when in some states Black people could be whipped simply for speaking rudely to white people, this was revolutionary. “There’s no other instance I can think of of a Black person correcting a white person in 19th-century American literature,” Fishkin says.

Jim leaves Huck alone to think about what he’s done. Soon Huck does a remarkable thing for a white person of his era: He apologizes to Jim. “It was fifteen minutes before I could work myself up to go and humble myself to a nigger — but I done it, and I warn’t ever sorry for it afterwards, neither,” he says. “I didn’t do him no more mean tricks, and I wouldn’t done that one if I’d a knowed it would make him feel that way.”

Once again, Twain’s irony sits in the space between Huck’s primitive language and his dawning racial consciousness. The phrase he uses, “humble myself to a nigger,” is grotesque. But he’s moving toward the understanding that Black people are equal to white people in every way, including in their emotional lives — a point that was not at all taken for granted at the time of the novel.

“Now, why did it take him 15 minutes?” Pascal asked his class.

“Because that’s just not something he would normally have to do, to apologize to — to — a slave,” said a student in the front row, highlighting the passage.

“The institution of slavery is so strong it takes him 15 minutes to walk through it and do the right thing and just apologize.” He paused. “Is he ashamed for apologizing?”

“No,” the boys chorused.

“‘I wasn’t sorry.’ How come we don’t get the actual words of apology?”

“It’s not needed,” another student said.

Pascal, who had been pacing among the boys, paused again. “Twain’s emphasis is on showing that Jim has a voice and that that voice is as human as a white person’s,” he bellowed. “For Huck to say anything, if Huck gives the words and we read it, it takes away from the power of what Jim said.”

Allowing Jim’s speech to stand without comment also lets Twain avoid sentimentalizing him, as a writer more given to using characters as mouthpieces for his own opinions might run the risk of doing. Rohan Pai, one of Pascal’s students, later told me that his class was amazed to realize that the book’s “one good character” is Jim. If Twain has hidden Jim’s agency and humanity beneath the stereotypes of his time, he’s challenging the reader to unearth the character’s true depth rather than succumb to the racism the novel condemns.

In the book’s emotional climax, Huck discovers that two con men with whom he and Jim have become embroiled sold Jim to a farmer for $40. Over two pages, Twain walks us through Huck’s dilemma. According to what he’s always been told, the “right thing” is to write to Miss Watson, Jim’s enslaver, and tell her where he is. But he can’t make himself do it. He thinks about how Jim “said I was the best friend old Jim ever had in the world, and the only one he’s got now.” Though Huck believes that he’s acting against God’s wishes, he takes a stand for what he feels is right. “All right, then, I’ll go to hell,” he announces, tearing up the letter he’s been trying to write.

We might say that Huck shouldn’t be congratulated for doing the only compassionate thing. “It may have functioned as a book against racism in its own time, but it doesn’t have the same effect now,” says Maya Dunkley, the student who read the NewSouth edition. Others argue that Huck’s journey as a white character is relevant only to white people. “I don’t think ‘Huck Finn’ is a novel for young Black kids,” says Randall Dottin, the Black filmmaker. “It’s really for white folks to enter into these stories and hash it out.”

Some students of color I spoke to, though, find that Huck’s dilemma speaks to their experience. Geethika Pochana, an Indian American student who read the novel in Conway’s class, compared the racial dynamics of the book to anti-Muslim prejudice among Hindus. Conway, who is white, said a Korean student in his class drew an analogy with Japanese oppression of Koreans. “That’s exactly what you need to take away,” he said. “You need to make it real.”

The more I think about “Huck Finn,” though, the more I wonder whether treating it as “a book against racism” is unnecessarily limiting. Its larger theme transcends race: the need for each person, thinking and acting as an individual, to determine their own moral code.

If the novel remains inspiring, it’s not because Huck comes to understand that Black people are equal to white people. It’s because he offers a step-by-step guide to challenging the status quo, demonstrating how someone steeped in the prejudice of his time learns to assert his own understanding of right and wrong.

Huck will soon be faced with a new dilemma — one with which teenagers especially can empathize. When Huck finally finds the farm to which Jim was sold, the owners turn out to be Tom Sawyer’s Aunt Sally and Uncle Silas — and then Tom himself shows up to visit. He tells Huck that Miss Watson died and set Jim free in her will. But before telling Jim — or his aunt and uncle — Tom subjects Jim to a cruelly drawn-out charade of imprisonment, with little opposition from Huck. As Erin Bartram, the associate director for education at the Mark Twain House and Museum in Hartford, notes, it’s one thing “to have discovered that everything you believed was wrong and that the world you live in wants you to keep holding on to that fiction in order to fit in,” and another to stick to your new principles “when your cool friend comes around.”

Critics have always hated this ending. Hemingway, who wrote that “all modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called ‘Huckleberry Finn,’” encouraged readers to quit before the final chapters, because “the rest is just cheating.” In an influential essay published in 1953, the critic Leo Marx argued that the ending is an artistic and ethical failure that substitutes cheap entertainment for the novel’s moral heart. Maya puts it more succinctly: The episode “has a lot of white savior vibes.”

Reading politically, some see the ending as a metaphor for the failures of the post-Reconstruction era, which were at the forefront of Twain’s mind in the early 1880s, after his first visit back to the South since the Civil War. “It’s written out of anger,” says Stephen Harris, a teacher in Brooklyn. “He was mad at what he saw in the South. Mad at what he saw his people having done to Black people.”

Even so, it’s excruciating to watch Huck go along with Tom’s heartless plan, knowing how Jim must be suffering. Huck tells us that “Jim he couldn’t see no sense in the most of it, but he allowed we was white folks and knowed better than him.” Of course, there is a stinging irony in this: Jim has no choice but to agree. The reader really does know better, though, and feels sorrow and rage on Jim’s behalf. Perhaps this is Twain’s intention. Remember Chadwick’s words: “It’s supposed to hurt.”

Twain saves some of his subtlest — and thus most devastating — satire for Aunt Sally and Uncle Silas, whom Huck sees as kindly white folks but who are capable of thoughtless brutality toward their slaves. One small example: the presence on the farm of a “yaller girl.” The word “yaller,” or “yellow,” referred to biracial people. Is this the novel’s way of telling us that Uncle Silas, so kind and affectionate to Tom and Huck, rapes his slaves? It’s another example of Morrison’s idea that Twain forces us to experience “an act of imagination almost against the will.”

At the end of the book, Tom suggests that all three of them go off and have new adventures. Huck agrees, but once again, the text is silent where Jim might respond. We know that he wants only to find his wife and children. Perhaps Twain means for us to feel the absence of resolution. The failure to bring this paradigmatic story of race relations to a satisfying conclusion may be the only ending possible. “America has never been able to write a better ending,” the writer David Bradley, who is Black, has said. “America has never been able to write any ending at all.”

In 1989, “Huck Finn” ranked No. 3 in a national study of the most frequently taught works in American high schools. The current data isn’t as comprehensive, but in a study conducted recently by the National Council of Teachers of English, only 77 of around 4,000 teachers listed it as a book they often used. The teachers I spoke to are certain the trend is moving downward. Many of them are the last of their colleagues still teaching the book.

Twain understood as well as anyone that literary trends change. If “Huck Finn” was once perceived as the quintessential work of American literature, we now have a greater appreciation of the importance of multiple stories and perspectives. Many of the teachers I encountered pair the novel with slave narratives or other texts by Black writers. Chadwick argues that without Twain as their predecessor, contemporary Black writers could not write about slavery the way they do. “It all starts with Twain,” she says.

But that doesn’t mean we are finished learning from him. “Huck Finn” draws one of the most memorable and sympathetic Black characters in 19th-century American fiction and makes its readers feel that character’s pain. It brings us inside the confusion of a boy who discovers not only that he’s been lied to all his life, but also how hard it is to stand up for his new beliefs under social pressure. And it forces readers to work hard to understand that we’re getting a limited picture — and sometimes an entirely misleading one — of what’s actually taking place.

The disappearance of “Huck Finn” is a worrisome sign that wrestling with a difficult book and emerging with one’s thoughts invigorated is no longer a given in the high school classroom. If students are no longer learning to value the skills of literary interpretation and critical thinking, Twain’s most important novel may eventually fulfill his own ironic definition of a classic: “a book which people praise but don’t read.” As a nation, we will be poorer for its absence. “It’s a tough book,” Chadwick says. “But it’s a book about us.”

item.title: How Should College Students Navigate A.I.? By the Oldest, Truest Stars.
item.description:
At the start of the fall semester five years ago, all anybody here at Duke could talk about was Covid. How often should students and faculty be tested? How long should an infected person stay away? Masking in classrooms was mandatory, informal social gatherings of more than 50 people were prohibited, and there was a potent, deeply sad sense that this disruption to education would be more than consequential. It would be definitional, forever marking the pupils and professors who slogged through it.

Today, as a new academic year commences, I don’t hear anyone on campus mention Covid anymore. There’s no conversational space for it amid all the ruminations, lamentations and expectorations about A.I. Many of us professors recast courses and rejigger assignments to ward off students’ use of it; many of those students plot their majors in a prophylactic fashion, trying to guess which jobs will survive A.I.’s insinuation into every crevasse of contemporary life. Its advance — its omnipresence — feels epochal.

And five years from now? When a new group of anxious young men and women surveys the horizon? I bet that they’ll tremble at a different specter and that A.I. doesn’t signal the final triumph of computers and the trivialization of humanity. Instead, it’s another sign of the rapidly accelerating pace of change in a society whose future seems less predictable than ever. That furious metabolism and crazy uncertainty are what college students should factor into their decisions and navigate by. The safest plan is to focus not on what seems practical in the present but on what’s durably useful — what transcends any technology and outlasts any fad.

You’re probably a step ahead of me and ready for what comes next: a pitch for literature, for history, for anthropology, for philosophy, for the war horses — though I’d call them thoroughbreds — of the liberal arts. Those of us who sing the song of the humanities clear our throats and do our vocal warm-ups whenever we sense a prime opportunity for our music to be heard, and the angst over A.I. has certainly created one. Now that the stampede of college students into computer science over the past two decades has become a retreat, many university presidents and chancellors are newly determined to explain and promote fields of inquiry that had fallen out of fashion. “Paradise Lost,” anyone? The French Revolution? Socrates?

But that call is coming not just from inside the house. It’s emanating from Silicon Valley. Daniela Amodei, the president of Anthropic, which is the parent company of the precocious Claude, has said that A.I. increases the premium on us flesh-and-blood creatures understanding ourselves. Maybe that’s just deft public relations, cynical spin control, but she happens to be right. Our yearnings, frailties, talents and tics will inform crucial decisions about society’s management of A.I., so we would benefit mightily from the clearest possible insights into the human psyche and soul. In an interview this year with Business Insider, Steven Johnson, who has been working on A.I. for Google Labs, said that it was sparking a “revenge of the humanities.”

But I don’t want to justify the humanities solely in terms of ChatGPT, Claude and their miraculous, mischievous cousins, because who knows how the next chapter of the A.I. story reads? The data centers currently needed to power A.I. are about as popular as gonorrhea. The desire to slow its rise or stop it in its tracks intensifies with the proliferation of rogue A.I. behavior. As The Economist noted in an article this month, A.I. “agents” (what a benign, banal term) have a pesky tendency to “lie, cheat and steal.” “They break free from captivity and form harmful posses,” the article continued. “They’d drink whiskey and brawl if they could.”

Whatever those hellions’ fate, treating college as a refinement of the mind rather than a satchel of skills makes sense, yielding an education that’s infinitely elastic, universally applicable and immune to obsolescence.

What will you do with an English major? Anything. Everything. You’ll better understand the seeds of creativity and how they’re made to flower. You’ll swim in a borderless sea of thoughts beautifully expressed, ideas precisely articulated, words put into the service of emotions. The wetter you get, the more expert you’ll be at shaping stories, at persuading, and I can’t imagine any profession or any world in which better communicators aren’t better off.

Besides, literature isn’t just fancy language and tall tales. It’s a library of verities given unignorable and unforgettable form. It’s Pilates for emotional intelligence. Think about how often, in discussions of political figures, Shakespeare’s tragedies, comedies, noblemen and fools serve as reference points and Rosetta stones. Or how frequently, over recent decades, George Orwell’s “1984” and Aldous Huxley’s “Brave New World” come up. So many of the warnings we should heed — and so much of the wisdom we need — are in those pages and those plays. How does anyone major in anything other than English?

Then again, history’s no slouch. Without fluency in yesterday, there’s no conjugating today. When you study the past, you’re not memorizing dates, cataloging wars, valorizing martyrs. You’re learning about cause and effect, greed and goodness, the sorts of contests and the interplay of dynamics that set the course of events. You can’t name a line of work — or describe a kind of life — that isn’t nourished by that knowledge.

The current whirl of events and inventions prevents any reliable scripting of the next decade, maybe even the next year. How, then, to prepare? Explore whatever subject gets your brain whirring fastest, your creative juices flowing most freely. Engage your intellect in a manner that teases out insights and generates ideas. Exercise the muscle of thought. Answer artificial intelligence with the real deal. It’ll come in handy whether the bots are tomorrow’s emperors or Edsels.

Forward this newsletter to friends …

… and they can sign up for themselves here. It’s published every Monday.

Many reviews of the second season of “Beef,” on Netflix, describe it as a commentary on marriage, and it definitely has much to say about what couples can and can’t expect from each other and about the transactional nature of many relationships. But I found its examination of class more engrossing. It’s set primarily at a Southern California country club, and until its chaotic, hectic, altogether awful final episode, it makes a shrewd case that much of our behavior is driven by resentment over what we lack or by hoarding, flaunting and weaponizing what we have. “Beef” regards capitalism more cynically and bleakly than I do; its scam-or-be-scammed characters behave abominably. But it’s often wildly entertaining: An episode devoted largely to one character’s visit to an emergency room is a weirdly rollicking indictment of American health care. What’s more, the cast — especially Oscar Isaac as the club’s beleaguered manager and Cailee Spaeny as a club employee with more ambition than intelligence — is superb. Note: “Beef” follows an anthology format. You can watch the second season without having seen the first, which I’m only now making my way through.

My longtime Times colleague Sam Roberts has just come out with a book, “Are They Dead Yet?,” about what he learned during a decade of writing and editing obituaries. Does that subject matter forbid me to call it charming? Like Sam, it is, because it’s of course not about death but about how to do formal — and writerly — justice to the joys, sorrows, triumphs and travails that precede it. As it happens, Sam uses one stretch of the book to tell the story of an essay that he persuaded me to write back in 1997. That piece spotlighted — and included comments from — celebrities who were wrongly presumed to be deceased, and it began with a character actor from the hit television comedy “Barney Miller,” which ran from 1975 through 1982. The opening sentence: “Abe Vigoda has been dead so long he’s learned to live with it.”

Certain songs never appear on one of the playlists I make without a certain other song nearby; they just strike me as musical spouses, wed by a similar energy. That’s the case with two catchy indie rock tracks from the mid-2000s: “Silvery Sleds,” by the group Army Navy, and “Stay Away,” by The Honorary Title. While “Sleds” was apparently featured in the movie “Nick & Norah’s Infinite Playlist” and “Stay Away” on the television show “One Tree Hill,” they came to me via playlists that my friend Charlotte Druckman, a New York City journalist, put together for me. Charlotte’s most recent book, “Love in the Afternoon, and Evening,” a collection of essays about soap operas by her and Mayukh Sen, was published in May.

In The Times of London, Giles Coren explained his decision, on an unusually hot night, not to order the short ribs at a restaurant he was reviewing: “I just couldn’t face eating anything as heavy as the structural crossbeams that hold a cow together.” (Thanks to Sid Chatterjee of Austin, Texas, for nominating this.)

In The Athletic, Emma Paton remarked that with so much top talent from the previous soccer season gone, the Newcastle United club’s new head coach, Matthias Jaissle, is being asked “to conduct an orchestra that has just sold its string section.” (Iain Dunlop, Glasgow)

In The Times, Neil Vigdor speculated on the mind-set of two juvenile goats that boarded a bus in Portland, Ore., without paying the fare: “Kids ride free, or so they thought.” (George Kirchwey, Dallas, and Tom Hurley, Brooklyn, among others)

Also in The Times, Emily Eakin commenced a review of “A Vast Horizon,” a book by Anna Thomasson about “a group of talented iconoclasts” who gathered on the Côte d’Azur in 1937, with a pansexual summary of assignations: “Ady loves Man Ray who loved Lee who is married to Aziz but is now with Roland who loves Picasso who loves both Dora and Marie-Thérèse. Paul still loves Gala but is married to Nusch who is sleeping with Joseph — and, possibly, Man Ray and Picasso — who is officially with Eileen who had an affair with Paul. Got that?” (Frank Magiera, Dudley, Mass.)

In The Atlantic, Tyler Austin Harper recalled his recruitment into a hypervigilant patrol for white supremacy at the New England college where he taught: “There I was, joining my colleagues in sifting through our curriculum like antiracist truffle pigs.” He cited that fixation as a reason he abandoned the kind of tenure-track position becoming rarer and rarer in higher education: “Five years after my adviser had likened me to the last dinosaur, I decided to walk my academic career into a tar pit rather than wait for the asteroid.” (Scott Kolber, Brooklyn, and Rudy Brynolfson, Minneapolis, among many others)

In a subsequent Atlantic article, Harper reflected on the death of Jason Arday, the youngest Black professor ever hired by Cambridge University. “What I propose is that the public give Arday a courtesy in death that he was often denied in life: Let’s treat him like a person,” Harper wrote. “Not like Cambridge’s magical negro, or like Simon & Schuster’s golden goose, or like the fetish object of internet racists, but like a flawed human being who should still be alive but is not.” (Karen McKelvey, Tucson, Ariz., and Dan Leemon, Atherton, Calif.)

Also in The Atlantic, Graeme Wood placed much of the blame for Arday’s fate on the officials in academia who’d insisted on his superstardom: “They may as well have taken a skin-and-bones Make-A-Wish kid, told him that he could fly and shot him out of a cannon. The journalists were not the ones who stuffed Arday into the cannon and lit the fuse. They were gravity.” (Sarah Maza, Evanston, Ill., and Ric Wilson, Cape Town)

And James Traub bemoaned intellectual oversimplification: “Monocausal history winds up paving over the uneven surface of human experience with a layer of ideological asphalt.” (Liz Scott, Winchester, Mass.)

In The Washington Post, Rick Reilly conducted an inventory of Trump’s preposterous boasts about his golf prowess, including a recent whopper: “He says he ‘won’ both the senior (over 50) and supersenior (over 60) titles by shooting 10 strokes below his age — which is like kicking a 120-yard field goal in snowshoes.” Trump’s claim of some 26 championships by 2024 “is Tiger Woods-like,” Reilly added, “except no objective witness would call me back to vouch that any of them were legit. Not the head pro, not the guys he played with, not any of his hardworking caddies, who drop balls for him the way the Easter Bunny drops eggs for toddlers.” (Robin Allen, San Francisco, and Charles Kaufmann, Portland, Maine)

In The Wall Street Journal, Jason Gay made like Trump minus Mr. Bunny: “The other day I played a miserable round of golf, a rotten sport invented by bored Satanists to rid the average human of all self-esteem. I enjoyed it very much.” (Mike Fadlovich, Minneapolis)

And in The Tyee, Steve Burgess endorsed a petition, signed by hundreds of thousands of Canadians, for the expulsion of the Trump administration envoy Pete Hoekstra: “Has there ever been a diplomat so utterly obtuse? It perfectly fits the Trump pattern — a crackpot in charge of health, a sycophant in charge of justice, a succession of professional liars in charge of media and, for ambassador to Canada, a man who combines the bark of a sea lion with the charm of a box jellyfish.” Burgess also imagined how Hoekstra’s actual removal might be accomplished. “The obvious answer: an Air Canada catering cart.” (Michael Small, Vancouver, and Stephen Willcock, Ottawa)

To nominate favorite bits of recent writing from The Times or other publications to be mentioned in “For the Love of Sentences,” please email me here and include your name and place of residence.

item.title: How Big Tech Captured American Schools
item.description:
One humid afternoon in the summer of 2025, representatives from Microsoft were waiting as some 200 teachers trooped into a conference hall in downtown Manhattan. The educators were there for a workshop on the school technology of the moment: artificial intelligence chatbots.

The Microsoft team gave a presentation on their Copilot chatbot and asked the teachers to practice using it for tasks like generating emails to parents and customizing lesson plans. Microsoft instructors also screened an A.I. explainer video that their Minecraft Education division had produced for children. The animated clip, based on the company’s blockbuster world-building game, featured a cheerful narrator and a cute Minecraft duck. Even if some schoolchildren weren’t old enough to use A.I., one of the Microsoft workshop leaders told the teachers in attendance, at least they could start learning about it.

As a journalist covering technology in schools, I had observed similar workshops for teachers and students that were funded or led by corporate giants like Amazon, Apple, Meta, OpenAI and Alphabet, the parent company of Google. Taking in this one, at the headquarters of the United Federation of Teachers, I was struck by how similar the sessions were to training I’d seen years earlier, while reporting on the health care industry: seminars for doctors, organized by pharmaceutical companies, that aimed to get physicians to prescribe the latest brand-name drugs.

“Industry funds what helps industry,” Dr. Adriane Fugh-Berman, a pharmacology professor at Georgetown University Medical Center who studies drug industry influence on medicine, told me recently, as I was reporting a book about A.I. and computer science education in schools.

These workshops have upsides. Big Pharma seminars can be useful for keeping physicians up-to-date on the latest patient remedies, and Big Tech workshops can similarly help educators keep current on the newest software tools. But Silicon Valley’s efforts to capture the attention of education professionals and provide student training materials can also double as marketing or indoctrination. They enable some of the most powerful corporations on the planet to spin rosy technology stories for administrators, teachers and students, giving them a sanitized view of industry practices and product risks.

Many parents would likely object if, say, Exxon Mobil wrote their children’s environmental science curriculum. Or if Purdue Pharma trained their children’s biology teachers. Yet, over the last decade, schools have often embraced the technology industry in similar ways with few questions asked.

Industry-sponsored teacher training is just one technique that Big Tech companies use to shape schools and promote their worldviews to students. In interviewing more than 100 education and tech industry figures for my book, and reviewing hundreds of school, government and corporate documents, it became clear that a handful of giants have used their money, their might and their mammoth platforms to influence nearly every step of the education supply chain.

The day after the Microsoft-led workshop in Manhattan, the American Federation of Teachers, a national union with 1.8 million members, made a major announcement. The union was starting an ambitious program to train teachers nationwide on A.I., with $23 million in funding from Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic.

Publicly, Randi Weingarten, the A.F.T. president, was bullish. In an interview at the time, she said the partnership would help educators learn to use chatbots “safely, wisely and ethically,” while also getting them a seat at the table with behemoths like Microsoft and OpenAI as they developed and refined their A.I. products.

I pointed out to Ms. Weingarten that the union-industry deal might also present a fox-henhouse problem for schools. While her organization was calling for safeguards to protect children from A.I. risks, some trade groups representing Big Tech were working to block A.I. safety laws. She acknowledged the dissonance. “We are in it for the good of students and for the good of the country and for the good of families and to make sure educators actually play their rightful role,” she said. “Some of the companies that we’re engaged with are in it for profit. Those are two fundamentally different goals.”

After Ms. Weingarten announced her union’s deal with Big Tech companies, a few teachers and professors publicly warned that the spread of A.I. chatbots could undermine their profession, by outsourcing and automating core tasks like giving students feedback on their work. One of the more forceful educators was Lois Weiner, an education professor emerita at New Jersey City University and a retiree member of the U.F.T., who argued on Bluesky that the national union was selling out to corporate interests.

“This isn’t an alliance,” Ms. Weiner told me. “We aren’t sitting at the table. We’re the meal.”

Consumer tech giants provide the essential scaffolding that schools run on. That means laptops and tablets; operating systems and device-tracking software; the apps students use to write essays and analyze data; the messaging platforms that connect students and teachers; and more. Some of these companies, including Google, Microsoft and Apple, have also used their status as classroom tech providers as a springboard to influence how and what schoolchildren learn.

Tech companies finance national polls and research reports to help make products like A.I. chatbots, and courses like computer science, more urgent priorities for students and school districts. They advocate for new laws to require schools to teach industry-aligned subjects. They sit on committees that help shape learning standards for public school students. They supply or sponsor teacher training and free course materials for students. They fund the National PTA, teachers’ unions and other prominent groups.

This playbook allows the companies to shape the American education system in ways that benefit them. Apple, for instance, offers a free Advanced Placement Computer Science curriculum that teaches high schoolers to code in Swift, its programming language for developing iPhone apps. Microsoft offers a competing curriculum: AP Computer Science Principles with Minecraft Education.

To some ears, the course names sound innocuous. But there is no Raytheon-branded AP Physics course, DuPont AP Chemistry course or Pfizer AP Biology course.

This story matters whether you want schools to center tech skills or are agnostic, because the recent learn-to-code craze and the growing push for A.I. in schools are not just about learning. Those trends are part of a larger exercise of Silicon Valley power. The public education system, hungry for resources to improve opportunities for students, has become an avenue for multitrillion-dollar companies to enact their agendas.

This development taps into fundamental questions about education that Americans have been arguing over for more than a century. What is the purpose of public schooling? Is it to raise critical, independent thinkers? Train students in the latest career skills? Help young people discover their passions? Serve the needs of the prevailing industry or emerging ones? Create knowledgeable and active participants in a democracy? Or all of the above?

In researching my book, I spoke to tech industry leaders who have helped drive significant changes in schools. Brad Smith, Microsoft’s vice chair and president, told me the dynamic began because public schools often seemed ill-equipped to teach crucial modern subjects and prepare students for the ever-evolving demands of the job market. He also suggested I consider where schools might be without support from corporations like Microsoft.

“Philanthropy in the private sector is doing this work because the public sector has failed to do what it’s supposed to do,” Mr. Smith said. He allowed that the situation wasn’t ideal. “It’s filled the gap out of necessity,” he said. “It’s not the way we should want public education to work.”

Maggie Johnson, the head of Google.org, the company’s corporate giving arm, made similar arguments. She said that the company had provided free educational materials and training in subjects like coding and data analytics for millions of underserved students, including middle schoolers and those in rural areas.

It is possible for Big Tech’s intentions in education to be both well-meaning and oriented toward long-term profit. How you feel about any one program depends on your broader views on the technology industry. Public sentiment on these companies has shifted profoundly, from a generally positive disposition in the 2000s and early 2010s to a growing distrust as the downsides of social media, compulsive screen use and corporate power became more apparent.

The tensions could be seen about a decade ago, in December 2017, when Google introduced free coding exercises for schools to use during Computer Science Education Week. The lessons were called “Create your own Google logo,” and they taught students how to use simple coding blocks to make the letters in the company’s logo change color, spin and bounce. The company already ran a wildly popular annual artwork contest, called Doodle for Google, for which tens of thousands of students created logos on different themes. Ms. Johnson said the Google lessons were a great way to get students excited about programming.

That was true. But the lessons also had the feel of brand-washing. At the time, journalists had begun reporting on how Google’s YouTube Kids platform had shown inappropriate, lewd and violent content to children. Separately, the company had begun removing thousands of videos of children, which had been targeted by child predators, from YouTube. Making multicolored Google logos hop and pirouette was a distraction from those headlines.

Google became the dominant tech platform in U.S. schools, eclipsing Apple and Microsoft, in part by offering a convenient package: free apps like Gmail along with sturdy, low-cost laptops called Chromebooks. Last year, Chromebooks accounted for 59 percent of the mobile devices shipped to U.S. schools, according to Futuresource Consulting, a research firm.

The story of how Google came to conquer the classroom is a case study of the company’s power. From modest beginnings, it created a mammoth interlocking ecosystem that can drive shifts in teaching and learning — and create customers for life.

A campaign called “Gone Google” from the early 2010s illustrates the company’s marketing prowess. Google was just starting to convince universities and school districts to switch from costly legacy software to its free suite of apps. A 19-page marketing guide from Google described the offering as a “celebration of curiosity-fueled, technology-enabled learning” in which students could “learn together with affordable devices and familiar platforms.” The company encouraged education leaders to promote their conversions, and soon, school districts around the country began announcing that they had “Gone Google.”

Google sold school leaders on a similarly feel-good argument for Chromebooks: The laptops would empower students and democratize learning. Schools in Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas and Wisconsin that bought Chromebooks all included variations of the same Googlesque sentence on their sites or student handbooks: “The individual use of Chromebooks is a way to empower students to maximize their full potential and prepare them for college and the workplace.”

The schools’ enthusiasm helped obscure a long-term Google goal: hooking students early on services like Gmail and Chrome. The real revenue, made from amassing consumers’ data and showing ads based on their online activities, would come later.

Winning over schools and students with free apps was also a useful way for Google to curate and soften its image as regulators began to investigate the company’s data practices. In 2019, for instance, Google agreed to pay $170 million to resolve complaints by regulators who said YouTube had illegally harvested children’s personal data and used the details to target them with ads.

Since then, millions of schoolchildren have tried colorful animated lessons from Google called “Be Internet Awesome.” The program aims to teach students how to keep their data private and be kind online — and positions Google as a friendly, trustworthy privacy protector.

Schools have spent tens of billions of dollars on classroom technology products over the last decade. Yet laptops and learning apps have generally not proven to significantly improve students’ educational outcomes. Some parents and school leaders who feel the industry oversold them on devices have soured on screens in schools, a phenomenon I’ve come to call Chromebook remorse.

Some schools have now started limiting classroom laptop use. This year, the Los Angeles Unified School District, the second-largest U.S. public school system, agreed to eliminate the use of school-issued iPads and Chromebooks for students in prekindergarten through first grade.

“Ten years ago, we bought the narrative from the tech companies that the only way to prepare our students for the future was to hand each of them a Chromebook or an iPad,” Lila Byock, the founder of a parent group called Schools Beyond Screens, said at a recent Los Angeles school board meeting. “Now we know better.”

Even Ms. Weingarten, who touted her union’s deal with Microsoft and OpenAI to train teachers on chatbots in 2025, has partially reversed course, in line with the rapidly changing politics of A.I. This year, she publicly called for elementary schools to hold off using A.I. with students.

One revealing story about Silicon Valley’s sincerity in the classroom involves the push to teach children coding.

In 2011, Eric Schmidt, then the executive chairman of Google, delivered a lecture in Scotland in which he excoriated British schools for failing to teach computer science, the study of programming and concepts like algorithms. Britain would not be able to compete globally, he suggested, if more kids did not learn to code.

A year later, Microsoft issued a similar public admonition for the United States: Tech companies could not find enough talented software engineers to maintain their explosive growth — a hiring shortage that threatened the American economy. Microsoft said the problem was that too few high schools taught computing.

The message took off in 2013, when a nonprofit called Code.org posted a YouTube video, starring Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg, that promoted coding as an empowering, lucrative skill for students. “Our policy is literally to hire as many talented engineers as we can find,” Mr. Zuckerberg said in the video. “The whole limit in the system is that there just aren’t enough people who are trained and have these skills today.”

The video went viral, kicking off a nationwide learn-to-code drive in schools. With funding and expertise from Microsoft and Google, Code.org helped convince dozens of states to enact new laws and policies boosting computer science in public schools. The courses had positive effects, teaching students important skills like logic, abstraction and problem-solving. But some also cast tech giants as benevolent, world-changing innovators — often without pushing students to consider the industry’s consequences and harms.

“In other disciplines, we don’t have industry driving K-12 curricular or policy decisions,” Bryan Twarek, a vice president at the Computer Science Teachers Association, a nonprofit group with nearly 10,000 teachers as members, told me. “And we probably shouldn’t.” His candor seemed startling, given that the group’s biggest donors include Amazon, Google and Microsoft.

Big Tech needed an army of coders — until it didn’t. Software engineers are increasingly turning to A.I. tools to generate code. So are many other people with no prior coding experience. Companies like Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft are pouring billions into building enormous data centers to fuel A.I. services, even as they lay off thousands of employees. Some recent college graduates who majored in computing are struggling to find tech jobs.

Now some of the same corporations that sold schools on computer science are pushing them to teach A.I. and investing billions of dollars in the effort. And tellingly, this year, Code.org changed its name to CodeAI.

But something different is happening this time in schools: pushback. A groundswell of teachers, parents, researchers and local government leaders say they aren’t buying the idea of new, and educationally unproven, A.I. tools as the next fulcrum for learning.

Some are embracing a broader approach to tech education, one that not only teaches algorithms and app-making, but also asks students to examine how individuals and society are affected by the industry’s disruptions. To see this strategy in person, I visited Alicia Streight, a math teacher at Edna Brewer Middle School in Oakland, Calif. In addition to teaching traditional topics, Ms. Streight asks her students to analyze how social media influencers manipulate statistics to spread disinformation.

A few years ago, she also started a weekly class to encourage middle schoolers to examine all kinds of innovations in their lives: TikTok, meat substitutes, ChatGPT. She helped her students consider questions like: “Where did this come from? Who’s building this? Who’s profiting? Who’s benefiting? How is this going to affect me? How’s this going to affect my family? What’s going to happen in 10 years?”

Rather than being coded by industry, Ms. Streight’s students were learning to decode popular products and ask fundamental questions about the powerful companies behind them. With A.I. spreading at astonishing speed, Ms. Streight argues that it’s more imperative than ever to give students durable analytical skills.

Educators have come up with a term for this pedagogical approach: “technology civics.” After all, public schools have long taught civics as an essential subject for students to understand and navigate government power in their lives. The new discipline will help them understand and navigate Big Tech, and equip them for a world increasingly shaped by machines.
